hawaii.agency_name: Hawaii Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Services
hawaii.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Hawaii Revised Statutes section 587A-35, the family court may keep jurisdiction only until the youth turns 19.
hawaii.become_foster_parent: Apply through the Department of Human Services Child Welfare Services Branch, which works with its contracted partner to recruit resource families. Applicants complete a 15-hour pre-service training called HANAI, plus background and child abuse clearances, a home visit, references, and medical reports.
hawaii.benefits_after: Hawaii was the first state to extend Medicaid coverage to former foster youth until age 26. Through Imua Kakou, youth up to 21 can get monthly living assistance payments, medical and dental coverage, a case manager, help finding housing, independent living training, and help with jobs and education.
hawaii.extended_care: Yes. Hawaii's Imua Kakou program (Young Adult Voluntary Foster Care, Act 252 of 2013, Hawaii Revised Statutes chapter 346) lets young adults voluntarily stay in foster care until age 21. To stay in, the youth must sign a voluntary care agreement, meet monthly with a case manager, and be finishing high school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition.
hawaii.foster_overview: The Hawaii Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Services Branch, places children in foster care when a court finds they cannot safely stay at home. Licensed resource families (foster parents) give children a temporary home and daily care while the department works toward reuniting them with their parents or finding another permanent home.
hawaii.kinship_care: Yes. Hawaii's child welfare mission puts relative placement first, and relatives can become licensed resource caregivers for children in their family, including through child-specific licensing.

idaho.agency_name: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare
idaho.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Idaho Code section 16-1604, the court's jurisdiction over a child in need of care ends at the child's 18th birthday unless the court extends it.
idaho.become_foster_parent: Apply to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, Child and Family Services, for a state foster care license. The process starts with an information request and an orientation meeting, followed by an application, criminal background checks, pre-service training, and a home study.
idaho.benefits_after: Youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and the department offers independent living services for youth ages 14 to 21, including help with education costs through the federal Education and Training Voucher program. Youth in extended care who live on their own can use a Supervised Independent Living Placement, which pays a monthly maintenance payment to help with room and board.
idaho.extended_care: Yes. Idaho offers extended foster care to age 23 under Idaho Code section 16-1622 as amended by 2025 House Bill 245. A youth who turns 18 in department custody can stay in Continuous Foster Care until 23, or re-enter through Voluntary Post-18 Foster Care before turning 23, as long as they are finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do so because of a medical condition.
idaho.foster_overview: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, Child and Family Services, places children in foster care when a court gives the department legal custody. Foster (resource) families provide a safe, temporary home and work with the child's social worker and parents toward safely reuniting the family, usually within about 12 months.
idaho.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives can become licensed foster parents in Idaho, and a 2025 law (House Bill 245) gives the department more flexibility to license relatives, including expedited placement, limited variances, and separate licensing standards.

illinois.agency_name: Illinois Department of Children and Family Services
illinois.aging_out_age: Youth in Illinois can remain in DCFS care until age 21. Under 705 ILCS 405/2-31, juvenile court wardship ends automatically when a youth turns 21.
illinois.become_foster_parent: Apply through the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services by filling out the online foster parent interest form. Foster parents must be at least 21, pass criminal background checks for all household members, complete a home inspection and social assessment, finish 27 hours of PRIDE pre-service training, and complete a health screening.
illinois.benefits_after: DCFS offers scholarships for youth in care, along with housing, counseling, employment, education, and life-skills services, and youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26. Federal Education and Training Voucher funds are also available to help former foster youth pay for college or job training.
illinois.extended_care: Yes. Illinois provides child welfare services to youth in care past 18 until age 21, and a youth whose case closed can ask the court to reinstate wardship any time before turning 21. Youth in college with at least a C average can get assistance until 23, and a 2023 law (House Bill 1293) allows services to continue to 23 for a youth who is not yet able to care for themselves.
illinois.foster_overview: The Illinois Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) places children in foster care when a juvenile court finds they cannot safely stay at home. Foster families give children a temporary home and daily care while DCFS works toward reunification with their parents or another permanent home.
illinois.kinship_care: Yes. Illinois prioritizes placing children with relatives, and the Kinship in Demand (KIND) Act, signed February 5, 2025 and effective July 1, 2025, lets DCFS certify relative caregivers under separate standards so relatives can care for children in DCFS custody and get support.

indiana.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18, when regular foster care ends. Under Indiana Code section 31-28-5.8, a youth who was in court-ordered foster care on their 18th birthday can then choose extended care.
indiana.become_foster_parent: Apply through the Indiana Department of Child Services or a licensed child placing agency, starting with the inquiry form at IndianaFosterCare.org. Foster parents must be at least 21, pass fingerprint background checks, show they are financially stable, complete pre-service training plus first aid and CPR, and finish a home study; a foster home license lasts four years.
indiana.benefits_after: Through DCS Older Youth Initiatives, youth get independent living services starting at age 16, continued health insurance, case management, and help with housing, education, and jobs. Collaborative Care youth keep placement support and services to 21, Voluntary Services run to the day before turning 23, and federal Education and Training Voucher funds help pay for college or training.
indiana.extended_care: Yes. Indiana's Collaborative Care program is voluntary extended foster care from age 18 until 21 for youth who were in court-ordered care on their 18th birthday. The youth signs a Voluntary Collaborative Care Agreement, works with a case manager, and must meet school, job training, or work requirements; youth who left care can re-enter before age 20, and Voluntary Services continue to age 23.
indiana.foster_overview: The Indiana Department of Child Services (DCS) places children in foster care when a juvenile court finds them to be Children in Need of Services (CHINS). Foster (resource) parents provide 24-hour care in their homes while DCS works toward reuniting the child with family or finding another permanent home.
indiana.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives get priority as placements, and unlicensed relative or kinship homes can care for a child while working toward a foster license; DCS also runs Kinship Indiana support services for relative caregivers.

iowa.agency_name: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services
iowa.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Iowa Code section 234.1, a youth who is still in high school full time or in special education can still count as a 'child' for foster care purposes at age 18 or 19.
iowa.become_foster_parent: Apply through the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services or its foster recruitment contractors, Four Oaks Family Connections and Lutheran Services in Iowa. Foster parents must be at least 21, complete 30 hours of pre-service training, pass background checks, and finish a home study with home visits.
iowa.benefits_after: The Iowa Aftercare Services Network gives former foster youth ages 18 to 20 voluntary aftercare support, including a self-sufficiency advocate, life-skills help, and vendor payments, plus a monthly Preparation for Adult Living (PAL) stipend for youth in college, job training, or working full time. Youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and Education and Training Voucher funds help pay for college or training.
iowa.extended_care: Iowa does not offer a general extended foster care program to age 21. Instead, a youth age 18 to 20 who was in court-ordered foster care at 18 and is at imminent risk of homelessness or of not graduating from high school can apply to HHS for extended foster care or supervised apartment living, and all former foster youth can use voluntary Aftercare services to age 21, with Extended Aftercare to age 22.
iowa.foster_overview: The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) places children in foster care when a juvenile court finds them to be Children in Need of Assistance (CINA). Foster (resource) families provide temporary care, and the first goal is always to safely reunite the child with their parents; relatives are considered for placement first.
iowa.kinship_care: Yes. Iowa places children with adult relatives first, before other foster homes, and relatives can apply for a foster family license so they can receive foster care payments; relatives who take legal guardianship of a child from foster care may also qualify for the subsidized guardianship program.

kansas.agency_name: Kansas Department for Children and Families
kansas.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Kansas Statutes section 38-2203, court jurisdiction can continue until June 1 of the school year in which the youth turns 18 if they are still in high school, and until age 21 if there is no court-approved transition plan.
kansas.become_foster_parent: Choose a licensed child placing agency, such as KVC, TFI Family Services, or Saint Francis Ministries, to sponsor your application, and DCF's Foster Care Licensing Division issues the license. Applicants must be at least 21, have enough income to meet their family's basic needs, pass background checks, complete 30 hours of pre-service (MAPP) training, and pass a family assessment and home inspection.
kansas.benefits_after: Former foster youth in Kansas keep Medicaid (KanCare) coverage until age 26, can get Education and Training Voucher funds for up to five years (to age 26), and can have college tuition and fees waived under the Kansas Foster Child Education Assistance Act. The Independent Living Program also offers a monthly subsidy, start-up funds for housing, and help with transportation and school costs until age 21.
kansas.extended_care: Kansas does not offer a general extended foster care placement program to age 21. Instead, the court can keep jurisdiction until age 21 when no transition plan has been approved, and youth who leave care at 18 get help through DCF's Independent Living and Self-Sufficiency Program until age 21, including a monthly subsidy, Chafee funds, and help with housing and education.
kansas.foster_overview: The Kansas Department for Children and Families (DCF) oversees foster care for children a court has found to be in need of care when their parents cannot meet their safety needs. Foster children are placed most often with relatives or licensed family foster homes, and private agencies under contract with DCF handle case planning, placement, and foster parent recruitment and training.
kansas.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives can become licensed foster parents in Kansas, with an accelerated process for relative and non-related kinship homes and waivers for some non-safety licensing rules; kinship caregivers complete a 30-hour Kinship Path training course within the first year of licensure.

kentucky.agency_name: Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Department for Community Based Services
kentucky.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Kentucky Revised Statutes section 620.140, a commitment to the Cabinet cannot extend past age 18 unless the youth elects to extend it.
kentucky.become_foster_parent: Contact the local Department for Community Based Services office to start the process. Foster parents must be at least 21, attend an informational meeting, complete 15 hours of approved classroom training plus 15 hours of web-based pre-service training, pass FBI, sex offender registry, and child abuse registry background checks, and complete a home study; the process usually takes six to nine months.
kentucky.benefits_after: Through the KY RISE program, youth in care ages 16 to 21 get independent living help, and former foster youth can use the Tuition Waiver for Foster and Adopted Children, which waives tuition and mandatory fees at Kentucky's public universities and community and technical colleges. Youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and Education and Training Voucher funds help pay for college or training.
kentucky.extended_care: Yes. Kentucky's Extended Commitment program lets a youth who turns 18 in state care ask to stay in care until age 21 to receive transitional living support, including housing, help with daily needs, and case management. The youth must ask before turning 19, get court approval with the Cabinet's agreement, and be working full time (at least 30 hours a week), attending school full time, working part time while attending school part time, or have a documented disability that prevents work or school.
kentucky.foster_overview: The Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Department for Community Based Services (DCBS), places children in foster care when a court commits them to the Cabinet's custody. Foster families give children a temporary home and daily care while DCBS works toward reuniting them with their parents or finding another permanent home.
kentucky.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives and fictive kin can become foster parents for a child in their family, and relative or fictive kin foster parents need only be 18. Kentucky's KY KINS program offers peer support, training, and a kinship support line for relative caregivers, along with help such as child care assistance.

louisiana.agency_name: Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services
louisiana.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18. Under Louisiana Children's Code Article 686, a judgment placing a child in foster care stays in force only until the child's 18th birthday.
louisiana.become_foster_parent: Contact the Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services or a licensed child-placing agency and attend an orientation meeting to start certification. Applicants must be at least 21, have enough income to meet their own family's needs, be in good physical, emotional, and mental health, pass fingerprint background checks, complete about 21 hours of pre-service training, and finish a home study.
louisiana.benefits_after: Louisiana's Chafee Foster Care Independence Program serves youth in and formerly in foster care up to age 26, with Education and Training Voucher help available until age 23, and youth who age out keep Medicaid coverage until age 26. Extended foster care youth get intensive LifeSet case management help with education, employment, housing, and independent living skills.
louisiana.extended_care: Yes. Louisiana's Extended Foster Care program (Louisiana Revised Statutes section 46:288.3, signed into law in June 2019) lets youth who turn 18 in foster care voluntarily stay in care until age 21. The youth signs a voluntary placement agreement and must be finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition; caseworkers use the Youth Villages LifeSet model for intensive, weekly support.
louisiana.foster_overview: The Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) places children in foster care when a court finds them to be Children in Need of Care. Foster and adoptive (resource) parents give children a temporary home and daily care while DCFS works toward reuniting them with their parents or finding another permanent home.
louisiana.kinship_care: Yes. When a child is removed, DCFS must make reasonable efforts to place the child with a relative for kinship foster care, and an approved kinship foster parent receives the full foster care rate under Louisiana Revised Statutes section 46:286.1; DCFS also runs a Kinship Navigator program for relative caregivers.

maine.agency_name: Maine Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Child and Family Services
maine.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18, but they can choose to keep receiving care and support by signing a voluntary agreement with the department under Maine Revised Statutes Title 22, section 4037-A.
maine.become_foster_parent: Contact the Office of Child and Family Services or its recruitment partner, A Family for ME, and attend an informational meeting before applying. Resource parents must be at least 21 and Maine residents, and licensing requires an application, background checks, a home inspection, a home study, and introductory training.
maine.benefits_after: Maine's Youth Transition Services (Chafee Foster Care Independence Program) help youth with housing, education, employment, and life skills, and former foster youth keep MaineCare (Medicaid) coverage until age 26. Youth who were adopted or entered permanency guardianship at age 16 or older may also get Education and Training Voucher funds for college or training.
maine.extended_care: Yes. Maine's Voluntary Extended Support (V9) agreement lets a youth who turned 18 in state care keep placement and supports until their 23rd birthday (extended from age 21 effective August 8, 2023). To stay in, the youth must be working toward a high school diploma or GED, enrolled in college or career training, in an employment support program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do so because of a documented medical or behavioral health condition, and can re-enter before 23 if they left earlier.
maine.foster_overview: The Maine Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Child and Family Services (OCFS), places children in foster care when a court removes them from home for their safety. Licensed resource (foster) parents give children a temporary home and daily care while OCFS works toward reuniting them with their parents or finding another permanent home.
maine.kinship_care: Yes. Whenever possible, OCFS places children with relatives first, and relatives can become licensed resource parents for a child in their family; relatives interested in caring for a child should contact the child's caseworker or A Family for ME.

maryland.aging_out_age: Youth can remain in out-of-home placement under a voluntary placement agreement until age 21 under Maryland Family Law section 5-525. Court commitment as a Child in Need of Assistance ends at 18, but voluntary care continues past 18.
maryland.become_foster_parent: Contact the local Department of Social Services in the county where you live to start the process of becoming a resource parent. Applicants must be at least 21 and a U.S. citizen or legal resident, complete 27 hours of pre-service training, pass state and federal criminal background checks, have medical exams, and pass health and fire inspections of the home.
maryland.benefits_after: Maryland's Ready by 21 program serves youth in care from age 14 to their 21st birthday with help in education, employment, housing, finances, health care, and mentors, plus independent living aftercare services for ages 18 to 21. Former foster youth can also use the Tuition Waiver for Foster Care Recipients at Maryland public colleges, keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, and get Education and Training Voucher funds for college or training.
maryland.extended_care: Yes. Maryland offers extended foster care to age 21 through a voluntary placement agreement: eligible youth stay in placement automatically for 180 days after turning 18, and longer if the juvenile court finds it is in their best interest. To stay in, the youth must be finishing school, enrolled in college or job training, in an employment program, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do so because of a medical condition, and former foster youth can re-enter care before age 20 and 6 months.
maryland.foster_overview: The Maryland Department of Human Services, Social Services Administration, oversees foster care (called out-of-home care), which local Departments of Social Services provide. When a juvenile court finds a child to be a Child in Need of Assistance (CINA), the child is placed with a resource (foster) parent or kin while the local department works toward reunification or another permanent home.
maryland.kinship_care: Yes. Maryland follows a 'kin-first' approach that gives relatives and kin priority for placement, and since December 2024 the state has separate kinship licensing standards (Social Services Administration policy SSA-CW #24-06). Relatives can become licensed (restricted) caregivers for children in their family and get extra support and benefits beyond the child's social worker.
sources: https://www.dhr.maryland.gov/documents/SSA Policy Directives/Child Welfare/SSA 24-06 - Kinship Care Licensing Standards Policy.pdf
